# Wirecard and Jan Marsalek: Evidence-Bounded Reconstruction of the Public-Fraud Trail

## Executive summary

The returned benchmark evidence supports only a partial reconstruction of the Wirecard public-fraud trail. It establishes a documented sequence around Wirecard’s **28 April 2020 public statement concerning KPMG’s special investigation**, together with a later **European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study** that assessed broader weaknesses in corporate governance, auditing, financial-reporting oversight, and market supervision.

The evidence does **not** establish, from the returned sources:

- the reported or alleged €1.9 billion missing from trustee accounts;
- the date or content of Wirecard’s 18 June 2020 disclosure;
- an EY audit qualification, refusal to sign, or inability to verify bank balances;
- Wirecard’s insolvency filing;
- official ESMA, BaFin, FREP, Bundestag, prosecutorial, or law-enforcement findings;
- the date, circumstances, destination, or legal significance of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance; or
- a proven causal relationship between Marsalek’s disappearance and any accounting, supervisory, or criminal event.

Those matters must therefore remain unresolved in this evidence set. Adding them from general knowledge would violate the requirement to rely only on benchmark-returned evidence.

The strongest supported chronology is narrower:

1. On 28 April 2020, Wirecard announced that it had received KPMG’s report on a special investigation.
2. Wirecard said that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that no significant findings required adjustments to the 2016–2018 accounts.
3. The same announcement acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data required under its increased forensic requirements to prove earlier Third Party Acquiring revenues because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties.
4. Wirecard also acknowledged documentation and organizational weaknesses and announced a delay to its annual accounts and annual press conference.
5. A November 2020 study by the European Parliament’s Economic Governance Support Unit interpreted the broader Wirecard episode as involving failures across five “lines of defence”: internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing, and BaFin. That assessment is explicitly the authors’ opinion, not an official finding of the European Parliament or BaFin.

## Scope and evidentiary method

### Returned sources

Only two unique benchmark source IDs were returned:

- [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation), a Wirecard corporate announcement concerning KPMG’s special investigation.
- [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf), a European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study on the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case.

The source set is therefore not sufficient to reconstruct the entire historical case. It supports a limited chronology and a disciplined distinction between:

- **verified facts about what a source says or publishes**;
- **corporate assertions made by Wirecard**;
- **interpretations and assessments by the authors of SRC-002**; and
- **matters for which no returned evidence is available**.

### Source hierarchy

[SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation) is primary evidence of what Wirecard publicly disclosed. It is not, by itself, independent confirmation that all of Wirecard’s characterizations of KPMG’s work were correct.

[SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf) is an institutional policy study prepared for the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs. However, the document expressly states that its opinions are the authors’ responsibility and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament. It also states that the views of the relevant author do not represent a position taken by BaFin.

## Chronology supported by the returned evidence

### 28 April 2020: Wirecard announces KPMG’s special-investigation report

[SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation) states that Wirecard received KPMG’s special audit report in the early hours of 28 April 2020 and would publish it as soon as possible under its transparency website.

The announcement is identified as a disclosure of inside information under Article 17 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation. That establishes the nature of the corporate announcement, but not the independent truth of every substantive assertion contained in it.

There is a source-level date issue: the URL contains the path `/2020/04/22/`, while the announcement itself states “28-Apr-2020 / 07:52 CET/CEST” and repeatedly refers to 28 April. The stated announcement date should therefore be used cautiously, while the URL-path discrepancy should be preserved rather than silently ignored.

### Wirecard’s characterization of KPMG’s conclusions

Wirecard stated that:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.”

This is verified as a statement made by Wirecard. The returned excerpt does not reproduce a complete KPMG report or an independent KPMG statement. Accordingly, the proposition should be classified as **Wirecard’s characterization of the special investigation**, not as an independently verified finding.

Wirecard also stated that, across four areas—Third Party Acquiring, Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending, and business activities in India and Singapore—no significant findings had been made that required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts.

This supports the narrower conclusion that Wirecard publicly characterized the investigation’s findings as not requiring accounting adjustments in those areas. It does not establish that all relevant transactions, revenues, balances, or controls had been independently verified, nor does it establish that no weaknesses existed.

### TPA revenue verification and the evidence-standard distinction

The announcement contains two important statements about Third Party Acquiring revenue.

First, Wirecard stated:

> “In the course of the audits of the annual accounts for the years 2016-2018 the available documents and audit measures were sufficient for the proof of the revenues in the Third Party Acquiring business.”

Second, Wirecard stated that, under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements, not all data required to prove those revenues could be obtained because the relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties.

These statements should not be collapsed into one proposition. They refer to different evidentiary contexts:

- the documents and procedures available during the 2016–2018 annual-account audits; and
- the additional data sought under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements.

The evidence therefore supports a **difference in evidentiary standard and data availability**. It does not establish an outright logical contradiction, because information considered sufficient for an ordinary audit may not satisfy a more demanding forensic investigation.

Wirecard further stated that it had come to control the necessary data itself and had provided KPMG with more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 for forensic audit. Wirecard stated that this audit had revealed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances.

Again, the verified fact is that Wirecard made this statement. The excerpt does not identify the precise data, the relevant accounts, the audit procedures, or an independently reproduced KPMG conclusion. The statement should therefore be classified as a **corporate representation about the outcome of a forensic review**, not as a complete independent evidentiary finding.

### Documentation and organizational weaknesses

Wirecard stated that KPMG had identified documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period and that Wirecard had already identified those weaknesses itself.

This establishes that the corporate announcement acknowledged the existence of weaknesses. It does not establish:

- what the weaknesses were;
- which business units or individuals were responsible;
- whether they affected financial reporting;
- whether they affected the TPA business;
- whether they had been fully remedied; or
- whether they contributed to any later event.

Wirecard stated that it had been addressing those weaknesses since 2019 through a Global Compliance Organization and external consultants. That is evidence of a claimed remediation effort, not independent evidence that the remediation was complete or effective.

## Audit uncertainty and delayed financial reporting

### The role of EY in the returned evidence

[SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation) refers to the auditor as “E&Y” and states that Wirecard would coordinate with the auditor concerning completion of audit measures.

The source does not provide EY’s own statement. It does not establish:

- a qualified audit opinion;
- a refusal to issue an opinion;
- an inability to verify bank balances;
- a disagreement between EY and Wirecard;
- a conclusion that Wirecard’s accounts were misstated; or
- the final status of the annual audit.

Any such proposition must therefore be omitted from this reconstruction.

### Delay of the annual accounts and annual press conference

Wirecard announced that the release of the annual accounts and the annual press conference would not take place on 30 April 2020. It stated that it would coordinate with EY regarding when audit measures could be completed, taking account of COVID-related restrictions and completion of the KPMG report.

This supports three limited conclusions:

1. Wirecard publicly announced a delay.
2. Wirecard linked the timing to completion of audit measures, COVID-related restrictions, and completion of KPMG’s report.
3. The source does not state that those were the only reasons for the delay.

The delay is an important chronological signal of unresolved reporting and audit work, but it is not, by itself, proof of fraud or proof that the accounts were materially false.

## Missing cash and financial inconsistencies

### What the returned evidence does not establish

The benchmark-returned excerpts contain no evidence establishing:

- a missing €1.9 billion;
- the existence or status of trustee accounts;
- bank confirmations concerning those accounts;
- a shortfall between reported and actual cash;
- a specific accounting inconsistency involving cash;
- a 18 June 2020 Wirecard disclosure;
- a 22 June 2020 insolvency announcement; or
- a later restatement of Wirecard’s accounts.

Although the searches sought those subjects, the returned results supplied no additional source IDs addressing them. The absence of evidence in the returned source set is not evidence that the events did not occur. It means only that they cannot be asserted in this report under the evidence constraint.

### Relationship to the KPMG announcement

The evidence does support a limited connection between financial-reporting uncertainty and the 28 April announcement:

- Wirecard said that KPMG could not obtain all data required under increased forensic requirements to prove earlier TPA revenues.
- Wirecard acknowledged documentation and organizational weaknesses.
- Wirecard delayed publication of its annual accounts and annual press conference.

However, the returned evidence does not connect those matters specifically to missing cash, trustee accounts, or any particular later financial discrepancy. Any such connection would be an unsupported inference.

## Supervisory, regulatory, and institutional failures

### The five lines of defence identified by SRC-002

The November 2020 study [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf) states, in the authors’ view, that five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception failed “in one way or another”:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system;
2. Wirecard’s supervisory board;
3. External audit;
4. Oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing; and
5. BaFin as market supervisor.

The study describes its root-cause assessment as a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture. It argues that the existing framework was not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection.

These are significant institutional assessments, but their status must be accurately described. They are:

- not a court judgment;
- not a criminal-law finding;
- not reproduced as an official BaFin determination;
- not identified as an official ESMA finding; and
- not necessarily the official position of the European Parliament.

### Information flows and enforcement

The study’s policy analysis identifies information flow to markets and supervisors as an area requiring improvement. It refers to whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources and recommends stronger mechanisms for receiving and using such information.

It also recommends stronger accountability for external auditors, including stronger incentives to detect accounting manipulation and fraud. The study links this recommendation to the informational value and credibility of audits.

These passages establish the study’s reform assessment. They do not independently prove that a particular whistleblower report, short seller, auditor, supervisor, or institutional body received specific information and then failed to act.

### Internal controls and supervisory governance

The study recommends that listed firms be legally required to maintain an appropriate and effective internal control system. It also recommends that the head of internal control report to the supervisory board rather than management, and that internal-control audits be considered.

Those recommendations imply the authors’ assessment that existing internal-control arrangements were inadequate. They do not establish the precise structure of Wirecard’s internal controls, the reporting lines of any particular employee, or the responsibility of a specific individual.

### BaFin and FREP

The study argues that BaFin needed considerably stronger supervisory and enforcement powers, including forensic and investigative tools. It also proposes reducing the role of self-regulatory enforcement bodies such as FREP to a purely ancillary, optional function.

These are recommendations, not evidence that such powers were adopted or that a specific BaFin or FREP action caused a particular Wirecard event. The returned evidence does not contain the underlying official BaFin or FREP files, their timelines, or their conclusions.

## Jan Marsalek’s disappearance

### Evidence status

No returned source provides an official account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The benchmark results do not establish:

- when he disappeared;
- where he went;
- whether he left Germany;
- whether he was located;
- whether he was wanted by authorities;
- what role he allegedly played in Wirecard’s conduct;
- whether he possessed or removed information;
- whether he had a relationship with any intelligence, political, criminal, or commercial actor; or
- whether his disappearance caused, reflected, or followed any particular Wirecard event.

Accordingly, no factual chronology linking Marsalek’s disappearance to the audit issues, alleged missing cash, insolvency, or supervisory failures can be reconstructed from the returned evidence.

### Avoiding unsupported causal links

The existence of a public-fraud narrative involving Wirecard and Marsalek does not permit a source-free inference that:

- Marsalek caused the alleged financial irregularities;
- Marsalek knew about missing funds;
- Marsalek directed or concealed accounting manipulation;
- Marsalek’s disappearance demonstrated guilt;
- Wirecard’s audit uncertainty caused his disappearance; or
- supervisory failures enabled his disappearance.

Those propositions require evidence that was not returned. They should be omitted rather than presented as allegations unless a returned source specifically supports them.

## Evidence classification

### Verified facts about source content

The following are verified as statements or publication facts contained in the returned sources:

- Wirecard announced receipt of KPMG’s special-investigation report on 28 April 2020 [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- Wirecard stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- Wirecard stated that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts in the specified areas [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- Wirecard stated that not all data required under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could be obtained [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- Wirecard acknowledged documentation and organizational weaknesses [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- Wirecard announced a delay to its annual accounts and annual press conference [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation).
- The policy study assessed failures across five lines of defence [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf).

### Allegations or corporate assertions

Wirecard’s statements about the absence of incriminating evidence, the sufficiency of earlier audit materials, the December 2019 data review, and the absence of deviations between revenues and account balances are best classified as **corporate assertions about investigative or audit results**. The returned excerpts do not independently verify them.

### Interpretations and assessments

The claims that all five lines of defence failed, that the oversight architecture was flawed, and that institutional reform was required are **authorial assessments in SRC-002**. They should not be restated as official determinations by BaFin, ESMA, the European Parliament, a court, or a prosecutor.

### Unresolved uncertainty

The following remain unresolved within the returned evidence set:

- the actual financial status of the alleged €1.9 billion;
- the reliability of trustee-account confirmations;
- EY’s final audit position;
- the later course of Wirecard’s financial reporting;
- official supervisory findings;
- criminal or judicial findings; and
- Jan Marsalek’s disappearance and any connection to the Wirecard events.

## Contradictions and tensions between the sources or statements

### URL date versus announcement date

The SRC-001 URL includes `/2020/04/22/`, while the announcement itself is dated 28 April 2020. The body of the announcement should be treated as the stronger evidence for the stated publication date, while the URL discrepancy should be recorded as unresolved metadata inconsistency.

### Ordinary audit sufficiency versus forensic-data insufficiency

Wirecard said that available documents and audit measures were sufficient for the 2016–2018 annual-account audits, but that KPMG could not obtain all data required under its increased forensic requirements.

This is a tension between two evidentiary standards rather than a proven contradiction. The statement permits the possibility that ordinary audit evidence was considered sufficient while forensic procedures demanded additional information that was unavailable.

### No incriminating evidence versus identified weaknesses

Wirecard stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified while also acknowledging documentation and organizational weaknesses.

These propositions can coexist. Weaknesses in documentation or organization do not necessarily prove balance-sheet forgery. At the same time, the returned evidence does not establish whether those weaknesses were financially material or whether they later contributed to other events.

### Corporate characterization versus systemic assessment

SRC-001 presents Wirecard’s characterization of KPMG’s work. SRC-002 presents a broader authorial assessment that all five lines of defence failed in some way.

The sources address different questions and have different statuses. SRC-001 concerns a corporate disclosure about a special investigation; SRC-002 is a policy analysis of institutional oversight. Neither returned excerpt supplies enough underlying material to resolve whether the study’s systemic assessment is consistent with, or goes beyond, KPMG’s actual findings.

## Conclusion

The returned evidence supports a cautious public-fraud trail, but not a complete reconstruction of the Wirecard case.

The supported trail begins with Wirecard’s April 2020 disclosure about KPMG’s special investigation. That disclosure combined reassuring language—no identified incriminating evidence and no stated need to adjust the 2016–2018 accounts—with admissions of incomplete forensic data, documentation weaknesses, organizational weaknesses, and delayed annual reporting. Those elements establish public uncertainty and evidentiary limitations, but they do not themselves prove fraud, missing cash, or criminal responsibility.

The later policy study broadens the analysis from company disclosures to institutional oversight. Its authors concluded that internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and audit oversight, and BaFin each failed in some respect. That conclusion is an interpretive policy assessment, not an official adjudication.

The central missing links are precisely those needed to complete the requested narrative: official evidence concerning the alleged missing cash, the final audit position, insolvency, regulatory findings, and Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Because those materials were not returned by the benchmark tools, no responsible evidence-bounded report can assert those links.
